---
title: "Research is part of the job"
---

Two paragraphs, one string, two different results. Create a fresh app from the
template. Replace the `<h1>` in `index.html` with these
two lines:

```html
<p id="asText"></p>
<p id="asHtml"></p>
```

Now replace everything in `src/index.ts` with this:

```ts
const asText = document.querySelector<HTMLParagraphElement>('#asText');
const asHtml = document.querySelector<HTMLParagraphElement>('#asHtml');
if (!asText || !asHtml) {
  throw new Error('A paragraph is missing from index.html');
}

asText.textContent = '<b>bold?</b>';
asHtml.innerHTML = '<b>bold?</b>';
```

Start the app with `npm start` and look at the page. The same string went into
both paragraphs, and they do not look the same. Finding out why is your job in
this chapter, not the book's.

## Why this book stops explaining {#sec-research-why}

The web platform is documented already. Every element, every property, and
every event has a page written by the people who build browsers, and those
pages stay more current than any book. Copying a slice of them in here would
only go stale. So this book teaches the ideas and the vocabulary, then sends
you to the source for the details. You have met two of these stops already, in
the chapters on events and on the starter project.

The other reason is the exam. It runs on a computer with no internet and no
AI, and your own course material is allowed. What you looked up, understood,
and wrote down in your own words is what you carry into that room. Looking
something up once beats reading about it twice.

## MDN, the reference for the web {#sec-research-mdn}

MDN Web Docs is the site you used in year one for string methods, and it
covers far more than JavaScript. HTML elements, CSS properties, and the whole
DOM live there too. When a developer wonders what a property does, they type
"mdn" plus its name into a search box and land on the page.

Open [MDN's page for `textContent`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Node/textContent)
and read how the page is built, because every page in the reference follows
the same plan.

* The heading names exactly what is documented: *Node: textContent property*.
  `Node` is the general kind of object your paragraph is a special version of,
  so the page applies to your paragraph too.
* **Value** describes what you get when you read the property and what happens
  when you write to it. Under it sit short comparisons with the two properties
  that look similar.
* **Examples** are small pieces of code, written in JavaScript. Read them and
  rebuild the idea in your own file rather than pasting them.
* **Browser compatibility** is a table of browsers and versions. Everything
  this course uses is green there, so skip it until the day you try something
  brand new.

A page for a method, such as `querySelector`, is laid out the same way with
one difference: instead of *Value* it has **Syntax**, **Parameters**, and
**Return value**.

## A search engine {#sec-research-search}

MDN answers "what does this do". A search engine answers "why is my thing
broken", which is the question you actually have most of the time.

Paste the error message from the browser console into the search box and put
quotation marks around it, so the engine looks for that exact wording. For a
"how do I" question, write it the way you would ask a person and name the
technology in it: *how do I read the text a user typed into an input in
typescript*.

Then look at the date. A well-written answer from 2014 may describe browsers
nobody runs any more and recommend a way of working that has been replaced
twice since. An old result is still worth reading, and worth checking against
MDN before you copy anything out of it.

## An AI {#sec-research-ai}

An AI does the one thing the other two sources cannot: it explains at your
level. Ask it to say an MDN sentence again in simpler words, or to explain why
your own code behaves oddly, and the answer comes back written for you.

It can also be wrong while sounding completely sure, inventing property names
that sound plausible or answering about a version of a library you are not
using. Treat its answer as a lead, and check whatever you rely on against MDN.

Ask precisely. Paste the code you actually ran, then write what you expected
and what happened instead. "It doesn't work" gets you a guess back.

The coding buddy you set up in Part 1 is an AI that knows the rules of this
course, and two chapters from now you start working with it properly. It points
you at the source instead of ending your research for you.

## How a research box works {#sec-research-boxes}

A research box lists questions and stops there. The answers are not further
down the chapter. You find them now, with the three sources above, and you
write them down in your own words.

The exercise after the box needs those answers, and the quiz at the end of the
chapter asks the same questions again. Let the quiz drive you: answer what you
know, look up the rest, and come back until nothing is left open.

::: {.research title="`textContent` or `innerHTML`?"}
The exercise below shows text that a user typed, and you have to choose one of
the two properties for it. Find out:

1. A program sets a paragraph's content to the string `<b>bold?</b>`. What
   does the reader see with `textContent`, and what do they see with
   `innerHTML`?
2. Putting text that a user typed into `innerHTML` is dangerous. Why, and what
   is the name of the attack this allows?
3. Which of the two do you use to show text a user typed, and why?
4. Ask an AI the same question you asked MDN. Name one thing the AI added that
   MDN did not say, or one thing the AI got wrong.

For the exam, the rule for user text has to stick without looking it up.
:::

## Exercise: show what the user typed {#sec-research-exercise}

1. Create a new app from our template.
2. Replace the `<h1>` in `index.html` with this markup:

   ```html
   <label for="messageInput">Your message</label>
   <input id="messageInput" type="text">
   <button id="showButton" type="button">Show</button>
   <p id="output"></p>
   ```

3. Delete the starter's two lines in `src/index.ts`. Look up the input,
   the button, and the paragraph with `document.querySelector`, each with its
   element type, and throw an error when one of them is missing.
4. Add a click listener to the button. In the listener, write the input's
   `value` into the paragraph using `innerHTML`.
5. Run the app, type `<b>hi</b>` into the input, and click the button. Look
   at what stands in the paragraph.
6. Change that one line to use `textContent` instead. Type `<b>hi</b>` again
   and click. Compare what stands in the paragraph now.
7. Keep the property that belongs in this app. Above that line, write one
   comment naming the property and saying why this app uses it. Your research
   answers are the reason.
8. Run `npm run check` before you call the exercise done.
